text: Radiography is an imaging technique that uses X-rays, gamma rays, or similar ionizing and non-ionizing radiation to visualize the internal structure of an object. It has applications in medical settings, such as diagnostic and therapeutic radiography, and in industrial contexts for non-destructive testing. In conventional radiography, an X-ray beam generated by an X-ray generator is directed at an object, where varying amounts of radiation are absorbed based on the object’s density and composition. The transmitted radiation is captured by a detector, which can be photographic film or a digital detector, producing flat two-dimensional images known as projectional radiography. In computed tomography (CT scanning), an X-ray source and detectors rotate around the subject, which moves through the beam, allowing data from multiple angles to be collected and computationally processed into two-dimensional images on axial, coronal, and sagittal planes, which can be further combined into three-dimensional images. The origins of radiography and fluoroscopy trace back to 8 November 1895, when German physicist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays while experimenting with a Crookes tube wrapped in black cardboard; he observed a faint green glow from a barium platinocyanide screen 1 meter away, realizing invisible rays were passing through opaque materials. Röntgen named the radiation "X" due to its unknown nature and was awarded the first Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery. He produced the first human body image—a photograph of his wife’s hand—on a photographic plate, which she described as showing "I have seen my death." The first clinical use of X-rays occurred on 11 January 1896 when John Hall-Edwards in Birmingham radiographed a needle in a hand, and on 14 February 1896, he performed the first surgical use of X-rays. In the United States, Frank Austin at Dartmouth College identified Ivan Pulyui’s discharge tube as the only one producing X-rays in January 1896, and on 3 February 1896, Gilman Frost and his brother Edwin exposed Eddie McCarthy’s wrist to X-rays, capturing the image on gelatin photographic plates. Early medical use of X-rays occurred before the dangers of ionizing radiation were understood, with Alan Archibald Campbell-Swinton opening a radiographic laboratory in the UK in 1896. Marie Curie advocated for radiography in treating wounded soldiers during World War I. Initially, various professionals—including physicists, photographers, physicians, nurses, and engineers—conducted radiography in hospitals, leading to the development of radiology as a medical specialty. Radiographers now perform fluoroscopy, computed tomography, mammography, ultrasound, nuclear medicine, and magnetic resonance imaging. Early terms included "roentgenograms" and "skiagrapher," with the Japanese term "rentogen" sharing the same etymology. The body’s varying densities cause differences in radiation attenuation, with denser materials like calcium-rich bones absorbing more X-rays, enabling internal structure visualization. Radiographic anatomy is the study of anatomy using radiographic images. Medical radiography is typically performed by radiographers, with image analysis carried out by radiologists, though some radiographers specialize in interpretation. Projection radiography involves exposing an object to high-energy radiation and capturing the remnant beam as a latent image, which can be converted to light via a fluorescent screen, captured on film, or read via a phosphor screen (CR) or directly by solid-state detectors (DR). Bone and lung tissues are particularly suitable for this method, which is cost-effective and highly diagnostic. CT scanning uses ionizing radiation and computer processing to create cross-sectional images resembling slices of bread ("tomography"), with higher radiation exposure than standard X-rays, though modern technology has reduced both dose and scan time. Contrast agents are often used in CT and conventional angiography to enhance visibility of structures. DEXA (bone densitometry) uses two narrow, perpendicular X-ray beams to assess bone density, typically at the hip, lower back, or heel, providing a T-score value for osteoporosis screening; it is not used for diagnosing fractures or inflammation due to poor image quality and is also used to measure body fat. Fluoroscopy, a term coined by Thomas Edison, provides real-time moving images and is used to observe tissue or contrast agent movement or to guide procedures such as angioplasty, pacemaker insertion, or joint repair, often using a portable C-arm device in operating rooms. Biplanar fluoroscopy displays two planes simultaneously, improving efficiency in orthopedic and spinal surgeries. Angiography uses iodine-based contrast injected into the bloodstream to visualize blood vessels, detecting aneurysms, blockages, and new vessel growth, and is often used in balloon angioplasty. Contrast radiography employs radiocontrast agents to highlight structures in projection radiography and CT scans. Although not technically radiographic due to the absence of X-rays, modalities like PET and MRI are sometimes grouped under radiography because hospital radiology departments manage all imaging. Radiation-based treatment is known as radiotherapy. Industrial radiography uses X-rays or gamma rays to inspect manufactured components for internal defects, with gamma sources including 192Ir, 60Co, or 137Cs. Image quality depends on resolution (ability to distinguish closely spaced structures) and density (blackening power), with sharpness influenced by the size of the X-ray source; larger sources increase blurring. Radiation doses vary by procedure: a chest X-ray delivers 0.1 mSv, while an abdominal CT delivers 10 mSv. The American Association of Physicists in Medicine (AAPM) and other scientific bodies state that risks below 50 mSv for single procedures or 100 mSv for multiple procedures over short periods are undetectable or nonexistent, though organizations like the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) and American College of Radiology (ACR) maintain safety standards to minimize exposure. Lead is the most common shielding material due to its high density (11,340 kg/m³), stopping power, ease of installation, and low cost; photon shielding follows an exponential decay pattern, with doubling thickness quadrupling the shielding effect. Starting in the 1950s, lead shielding was used on patients during abdominal X-rays to protect gonads or fetuses, and dental X-rays to shield the thyroid; however, a consensus formed between 2019 and 2021 that routine lead shielding is unnecessary and may be harmful, though protection for medical staff and others remains recommended. Rooms housing X-ray equipment are lined with lead, with recommended thicknesses based on X-ray energy per the Second International Congress of Radiology. In response to public concerns, the Alliance for Radiation Safety in Pediatric Imaging, in collaboration with the Society for Pediatric Radiology, American Society of Radiologic Technologists, ACR, and AAPM, launched the Image Gently campaign to promote low-dose, safe imaging in children, which has been adopted globally and supported by equipment manufacturers. A similar initiative, Image Wisely, was launched by the ACR, RSNA, AAPM, and American Society of Radiologic Technologists to address radiation safety in adults. The World Health Organization and International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) are also advancing best practices to reduce patient radiation exposure. Evidence suggests that radiographs are used more frequently in fee-for-service dental practices. In medicine and dentistry, projectional radiography and CT images are referred to as "radiograms" or "roentgenograms" and "tomograms," respectively. Other X-ray sources include betatrons, linear accelerators, and synchrotrons; gamma rays are produced by radioactive isotopes such as 192Ir, 60Co, or 137Cs. Anti-scatter grids between patient and detector reduce scattered radiation, improving image contrast but increasing patient exposure. Detectors are categorized into imaging detectors (e.g., photographic film, image plates, flat panel detectors) and dose measurement devices (e.g., ionization chambers, Geiger counters, dosimeters). Each radiographic image includes a radiopaque side marker—such as an "R" for the right hand—to indicate the side imaged, either placed during exposure or added digitally if not included. Image intensifiers, analog devices using a vacuum tube with a caesium iodide coating, convert X-rays into visible images on a screen via electron emission and focusing. Digital array detectors, made of pixelated thin-film transistors (TFTs), are increasingly used in fluoroscopy and can operate indirectly (via scintillators like CsI) or directly (by capturing X-ray-generated electrons), with direct detectors avoiding blurring from phosphor materials. Dual-energy radiography, which uses two different tube voltages, is standard in bone densitometry and used in CT pulmonary angiography to reduce iodinated contrast dose.

Dual-energy radiography involves acquiring images using two different tube voltages. This technique is the standard approach for bone densitometry and is also employed in CT pulmonary angiography to reduce the amount of iodinated contrast needed.
